newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. sleuth asked to review text offending Islam.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sleuth asked to review text offending Islam.

text.p: Officials said on Friday the U.N. investigator on racism had been asked to take "corrective action" after fierce criticism from Islamic countries of a paragraph referring to the Koran in his annual report.

They said the request was forwarded in a letter from the chairman of the 53-member U.N. Human Rights Commission to the investigator, Maurice Glele-Ahanhanzo of Benin, but did not specify exactly what action he should take.
"However, the implication was that he should do something to satisfy the countries that found the paragraph offensive to Islam and the Koran," said one diplomat who followed the row.
"Some obviously want him to agree to cut it out retrospectively. But other countries on the commission say this cannot be done once it has been submitted."
The paragraph was an extract from an Israeli government review of anti-Semitic trends around the world which the Glele-Ahanhanzo, a lawyer, cited at length in his report.

It read: "The use of Christian and secular European anti-Semitism motifs in Moslem publications is on the rise, yet at the same time Moslem extremists are turning increasingly to their own religious sources, first and foremost the Qur'an (Koran) as a primary anti-Jewish source."

Islamic countries on the commission objected strongly to the phrasing, and the body, which ended its annual six-week session on April 18, eventually agreed by consensus that the paragraph should not have been included in the report.

The commission, despite reservations by Western members including the United States, also agreed after fierce debate to "express indignation and protest" at the inclusion of "such an offensive reference to Islam and the Holy Qur'an."
And it requested the chairman, Miroslav Somol of the Czech republic, to ask Glele-Ahanhanzo "to take corrective action in response to this decision."

U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut said earlier the letter had been forwarded to the investigator, who is now in Benin, asking him to advise Somol promptly of the action he planned to take "in the sense of the decision."

When the row broke out on the last day of the commission's session, Western delegations and some from eastern Europe argued that Glele-Ahanhanzo had included extracts from other reports that they did not like but they accepted that was part of his job.

But, diplomats said, when it became clear the dispute could block passage of an overall resolution condemning racism they agreed to go along with the consensus on condition the investigator was not specifically asked to remove the paragraph.

Glele-Ahanhanzo, the U.N. special rapporteur on contemporary forms of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, cited several other documents on these issues in his report, including one asserting that Arabs suffered discriminatory treatment in the United States.
It was not immediately clear how he would respond. Diplomats said he could point out that the paragraph was not his but express regret that its inclusion had offended some countries.
The commission passed a separate resolution last week calling for a major world conference to combat racism by the year 2001, subject to approval by the General Assembly.
